title: HEAT AND TEMPERATURE — Chapter 9, Class 11 Physics (Concepts, All 5 Scales & Step-by-Step Numericals)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Temperature vs Heat | Effects of Heat | Thermal Equilibrium & Zeroth Law | Thermometry | The 5 Temperature Scales & Fundamental Interval | General Conversion Formula | Numericals (Direct Conversion, Coincidence/Double-Reading Problems, Faulty Thermometer Problems, Arbitrary/Offset Scale Problems, Rankine & Absolute Zero Problems)

🌡️ TEMPERATURE — DEFINITION: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of all molecules present in a body. It tells you the DIRECTION heat will flow (hot → cold). Measured using a thermometer. SI unit: kelvin (K).

🔥 HEAT — DEFINITION: Heat is the SUM (total) of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance. It is a form of energy, measured in joules. Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until equilibrium is reached.

💡 KEY CONCEPTUAL DIFFERENCE (exam favorite): Temperature is an AVERAGE (intensive property — doesn't depend on amount of substance). Heat is a TOTAL/SUM (extensive property — depends on mass/amount). This is why a bucket of lukewarm water can contain MORE heat than a cup of boiling tea, even though its temperature is lower — more molecules means a bigger total, even if each molecule individually has less average energy.

⚡ EFFECTS OF HEAT — When heat is applied to a body, it can bring: (i) Change in temperature (ii) Change in volume (iii) Change of state of matter (iv) Electric effect (v) Generation of light energy (vi) Change in resistance.
⚖️ THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when NO heat flows from one to the other after being brought into contact — meaning they are at the same temperature.

📐 ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This law is what actually justifies using a thermometer — the thermometer is the 'third system'.)
🧪 THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM: A system that can be described using thermodynamic parameters — Temperature, Pressure, Volume, and Heat exchange.
🔬 THERMOMETRY: The science of temperature and its measurement. THREE MAIN STEPS: (i) Construction (ii) Calibration (iii) Sensitiveness.
═══════════ SECTION A: THE 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES & FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL ═══════════

💡 WHAT IS 'FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL'? It is simply the NUMBER OF DIVISIONS between the Lower Fixed Point (LFP — ice/melting point) and Upper Fixed Point (UFP — steam/boiling point) on a scale. This single number is the KEY to comparing any two scales, because it tells you how 'coarse' or 'fine' each degree is on that scale. A bigger fundamental interval = smaller, finer degree-steps.
📝 TABLE A1 — ALL 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES

| Scale | Symbol | LFP (Ice Point) | UFP (Steam Point) | Fundamental Interval (UFP−LFP) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Celsius | °C | 0 | 100 | 100 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Fahrenheit | °F | 32 | 212 | 180 | Relative (0 ≠ ice point) |
| Kelvin | K | 273 | 373 | 100 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |
| Réaumur | °R (Ré) | 0 | 80 | 80 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Rankine | °Ra | 491.67 (≈491.4) | 671.67 (≈671.4) | 180 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |

🔑 FEEL IT, DON'T MEMORIZE: Kelvin is just Celsius SHIFTED so that 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Celsius, fundamental interval 100). Rankine is just Fahrenheit SHIFTED so that 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Fahrenheit, fundamental interval 180). So: Celsius↔Kelvin is a pure SHIFT (add 273), while Fahrenheit↔Rankine is also a pure SHIFT (add 459.67). But Celsius↔Fahrenheit needs both a SHIFT and a SCALE change (×9/5) because their degree-sizes differ (100 divisions vs 180 divisions covering the same physical temperature range).

📐 GENERAL CONVERSION FORMULA (works for ANY two scales, including Rankine): (Reading − LFP) / (Fundamental Interval) is the SAME fraction on every scale, because all scales are measuring the identical physical temperature range between ice point and steam point.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Students often try to convert Rankine using the Celsius-style formula (Ra−0)/x. WRONG — Rankine's zero is absolute zero, NOT the ice point, so you MUST use (Ra−491.67)/180, matching Fahrenheit's fundamental interval of 180, not Kelvin's 100.
═══════════ SECTION B: DIRECT CONVERSION NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL B1: Convert 30°C into Fahrenheit scale.
Step 2: Substitute C = 30: 30/100 = (F−32)/180
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 30×180/100 = F−32 → 54 = F−32
✅ ANSWER: 30°C = 86°F
📝 NUMERICAL B2: Convert 98.6°F (normal human body temperature) into Kelvin and Rankine.
Step 2: Convert to Kelvin: K = C+273 = 37+273 = 310 K
Step 3: Convert to Rankine directly from Fahrenheit (same fundamental interval, just shifted by absolute zero): Ra = F+459.67 = 98.6+459.67 = 558.27

💡 TIP: Notice Kelvin was obtained from Celsius by a pure ADDITION (+273), and Rankine was obtained from Fahrenheit by a pure ADDITION (+459.67) — no multiplication needed, because each absolute scale shares its degree-size with its 'parent' relative scale.
═══════════ SECTION C: 'DOUBLE READING' & 'COINCIDING SCALE' NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: These problems don't give you a direct value — they give you a RELATIONSHIP between two scale readings (e.g., 'one reading is double the other' or 'both scales show the same number'). Assign a variable to the unknown common temperature, express BOTH readings in terms of that variable using the given relationship, plug both into the master equation, and solve.
📝 NUMERICAL C1: At what temperature will the Kelvin scale reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let temperature in Kelvin = 2F (since K is double F, as given)
Step 3: Substitute K = 2F: (F−32)/180 = (2F−273)/100
✅ ANSWER: At 176.69°F (i.e., 353.38 K), the Kelvin reading is double the Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C2: At what temperature will the Celsius reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let Fahrenheit = x, so Celsius = 2x
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 360x = 100x−3200 → 260x = −3200
✅ ANSWER: At −12.307°F, the Celsius reading is double the Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C3: At what point does the Kelvin scale reading coincide with (equal) the Fahrenheit scale reading?
Step 1: Let the common value be x, so K = x and F = x
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 100x−3200 = 180x−49140
✅ ANSWER: At 574.25 K (= 574.25°F), the Kelvin and Fahrenheit readings coincide.
📝 NUMERICAL C4 (Concept-challenging — physically impossible case): At what temperature would the Rankine reading equal the Celsius reading numerically?
Step 1: Let common value = x, so C = x and Ra = x
Step 4: Check physical validity: absolute zero is −273°C. Since −614.25°C is COLDER than absolute zero, this temperature CANNOT physically exist.
✅ ANSWER: No physically valid solution exists — the equality would require a temperature below absolute zero.
💡 TIP: ALWAYS sanity-check your final answer against absolute zero (−273°C / 0 K) when an absolute scale (Kelvin or Rankine) is involved — algebra can give you a number, but physics can reject it.
📝 NUMERICAL C5: At what temperature will the Réaumur scale reading be numerically equal to the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let common value = x, so Ré = x and F = x
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 180x = 80x−2560 → 100x = −2560
✅ ANSWER: At −25.6°Ré = −25.6°F, the two readings coincide.
═══════════ SECTION D: FAULTY / MISCALIBRATED THERMOMETER NUMERICALS ═══════════

📐 METHOD: A faulty thermometer has WRONG numbers marked at its LFP and UFP (instead of the standard 0 and 100 for Celsius, etc.), but it still divides the space between them into equal, proportional divisions. Use: (Faulty reading − Faulty LFP)/(Faulty UFP − Faulty LFP) = (Correct reading − Correct LFP)/(Correct UFP − Correct LFP)
📝 NUMERICAL D1: A faulty thermometer has its fixed points marked at 2 and 98 (instead of 0 and 100). What is the correct Celsius temperature when this faulty thermometer reads 20°C?
Step 1: Faulty LFP = 2, Faulty UFP = 98, Faulty reading = 20. Correct LFP = 0, Correct UFP = 100.
✅ ANSWER: The correct reading is 18.75°C.

📝 NUMERICAL D2: A thermometer is wrongly calibrated — it reads the melting point of ice as −10°C, and reads 60°C in place of the correct 50°C. Find the reading this faulty thermometer would show at the boiling point of water (correctly 100°C).
Step 1: Faulty LFP = −10°C. Correct reading (C) = 50°C corresponds to faulty reading (Cf) = 60°C. Find faulty UFP (x) using correct UFP = 100°C, correct LFP = 0°C.
✅ ANSWER: The faulty thermometer will read 130°C at the actual boiling point of water.
📝 NUMERICAL D3: The distance between the LFP and UFP marks on a thermometer is 80 cm. Find the Celsius temperature when the mercury level has risen 10.4 cm above the lower fixed point.
Step 1: 80 cm of mercury rise = 100°C (the full fundamental interval). So 1 cm = 100/80 parts.
✅ ANSWER: 13°C.
💡 TIP: This is really the SAME logic as the faulty-thermometer formula — physical length on the thermometer stem is just another 'scale' being converted into Celsius using the ratio method.
═══════════ SECTION E: ARBITRARY / OFFSET SCALE NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: These invent a brand-new, fictional scale with its own LFP and UFP (sometimes even its own fundamental interval). Treat it exactly like Celsius vs Fahrenheit — set up the ratio using the master-equation logic, don't panic just because the scale is unfamiliar.
📝 NUMERICAL E1: In an arbitrary scale, water freezes at 40° and boils at 290°. Find the reading on this arbitrary scale corresponding to 62°C.
Step 1: Arbitrary LFP = 40, Arbitrary UFP = 290, so fundamental interval = 250. Correct LFP = 0, UFP = 100 (Celsius).
Step 2: (C−0)/100 = (Cf−40)/250 where Cf is the arbitrary-scale reading
Step 5: Cf = 195
✅ ANSWER: 62°C corresponds to 195° on the arbitrary scale.
📝 NUMERICAL E2: A new scale 'X' has its ice point marked at −20°X and its steam point marked at 130°X. Find the reading on scale X when the Celsius thermometer reads 50°C.
Step 1: Fundamental interval of X = 130−(−20) = 150
✅ ANSWER: X = 55°X

📝 NUMERICAL E3 (Two unknown thermometers, no Celsius involved at all — pure ratio thinking): Thermometer P has LFP=10 and UFP=160. Thermometer Q has LFP=20 and UFP=120. When P reads 70, what does Q read?
Step 1: Use the ratio method directly between P and Q (skip Celsius entirely — it's not needed as a 'middleman', any two scales can be linked directly): (P−LFPp)/(UFPp−LFPp) = (Q−LFPq)/(UFPq−LFPq)
✅ ANSWER: Q reads 60.
💡 TIP: This problem exists to break a bad habit — many students think Celsius MUST be used as a bridge in every conversion. It doesn't. The ratio method works between ANY two linear scales directly.

📝 NUMERICAL E4: A scale 'Y' has the SAME fundamental interval as Celsius (100 divisions) but its ice point is offset and marked at 50°Y instead of 0. If thermometer Y reads 68°Y, find the corresponding Celsius temperature.
Step 1: Since fundamental intervals are equal (both 100), this is a PURE SHIFT relationship (like Celsius→Kelvin), not a scale-and-shift relationship (like Celsius→Fahrenheit): (C−0)/100 = (Y−50)/100
Step 2: Since denominators are equal, C = Y−50
✅ ANSWER: 18°C.

💡 TIP: Whenever two scales have the SAME fundamental interval, conversion is always a pure addition/subtraction (like Celsius↔Kelvin, or Fahrenheit↔Rankine) — no multiplication ever needed. Only DIFFERENT fundamental intervals force a multiplication (scaling) step.
═══════════ SECTION F: RATE / ERROR / RATIO NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL F1: A Fahrenheit thermometer reads 99°F when a standard Celsius thermometer reads 37°C. Find the error in the Fahrenheit scale.
Step 1: Convert 37°C to its TRUE equivalent in Fahrenheit: (C−0)/100=(F−32)/180 → 37/100=(F−32)/180
Step 3: Error = Faulty reading − True reading = 99−98.6 = 0.4
✅ ANSWER: Error in Fahrenheit scale = 0.4°F.
📝 NUMERICAL F2: A materials-testing lab thermometer reads only in °F. The initial sample temperature is 68.2°F, and it must be increased by 40°C. What is the final temperature in °F?
Step 1: Convert the CHANGE (not absolute value) using the ratio of fundamental intervals: 100 parts in °C = 180 parts in °F, so 1 part in °C = 180/100 parts in °F
Step 2: 40°C change = (180/100)×40 = 72°F change
Step 3: Final temperature = Initial + Change = 68.2+72 = 140.2
✅ ANSWER: 140.2°F.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Never apply the full C-to-F formula (×9/5, +32) to a temperature CHANGE/DIFFERENCE — the '+32' offset only applies to absolute readings, not to a change in temperature. For a CHANGE, only the ×9/5 (or 180/100) scaling factor applies — dropping this distinction is the single most common error in this topic.
📝 NUMERICAL F3: A Celsius scale reads 30°C when a standard Kelvin scale reads 300 K. Find the error in the Celsius scale reading.
Step 1: Find the TRUE Celsius equivalent of 300 K: (C−0)/100=(K−273)/100 → C=300−273=27
Step 2: Error = Faulty reading − True reading = 30−27 = 3
✅ ANSWER: Error in Celsius scale = 3°C.
📝 NUMERICAL F4: What are the temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit when 2/3 of the Fahrenheit reading equals 1/2 of the Celsius reading?
Step 1: By the question: (2/3)F = (1/2)C → F = (3/4)C

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) DIRECT CONVERSION between named scales → plug straight into the master equation (C−0)/100=(F−32)/180=(K−273)/100=(Ré−0)/80=(Ra−491.67)/180. (2) 'DOUBLE' or 'COINCIDE' problems → assign one variable to the unknown temperature, express BOTH scale readings in terms of it, substitute into master equation, and ALWAYS sanity-check against absolute zero. (3) FAULTY THERMOMETER problems → use the ratio (Faulty−FaultyLFP)/(FaultyUFP−FaultyLFP) = (Correct−CorrectLFP)/(CorrectUFP−CorrectLFP). (4) ARBITRARY/OFFSET SCALES → treat exactly like faulty thermometer problems; Celsius is not mandatory as a 'bridge' — any two scales can be linked directly. (5) CHANGE/DIFFERENCE in temperature → apply ONLY the scaling ratio (fundamental interval ratio), NEVER the additive offset (+32 etc.).
